editorial.commentary: 整理者阅读建议：先区分预训练数据、动作表达与微调方案，再查看具体任务和机器人本体。摘要中的总体提升不能直接推为触觉任务、任意新机器人或所有实验条件下都更好。
editorial.summary: OpenVLA 把视觉输入与语言指令转成机器人动作。作者报告使用 7B 模型和 97 万条真实机器人示范，并开放权重、微调与训练代码，关注跨任务策略及新设置下的微调。当前入库依据为 arXiv 摘要和元数据；摘要中的性能比较属于作者报告，尚未核对完整实验协议或独立复现。
editorial.title_zh: OpenVLA：开源视觉—语言—动作模型

Whilst tactile displays exist to simulate and manipulate all of these cues individually, little progress has been made constructing devices that can control multiple cues simultaneously. This paper presents a tactile display technology that offers both softness and temperature change.\n  A prototype display, based on particle jamming and the thermal transfer of heated and cooled water, is evaluated in terms of its ability to change both stiffness and temperature. Mechanical evaluations demonstrate controllable stiffness increase of 300%, whilst thermal characterisation showed strong surface uniformity and a range of achievable temperatures from 10°C up to 50°C, with closed-loop control maintaining a 0.2°C error from a setpoint. {"arxiv_id":"2611.08364","authors":["Chang Shi","Ann Majewicz Fey"],"categories":["cs.RO","cs.LG"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08364"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["reinforcement_learning"],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-05T17:42:31Z","rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor--critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73\\% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03\\% vs. 0.63\\%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.","title":"SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing","title_en":"SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08364v1","version":"v1","version_updated_at":"2026-11-05T17:42:31Z"}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.08295","authors":["Gabriel Parra","Kimia Khoshnami","Daniel S. Brown","Laura A. Hallock"],"categories":["cs.RO","cs.HC","cs.LG"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08295"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-05T16:55:55Z","rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"Robot-mediated rehabilitation has the potential to deliver high-intensity, individualized therapy, but existing systems (which have not consistently improved outcomes) typically prescribe kinematic trajectories rather than explicitly targeting the neuromotor activations thought to support recovery. To address this gap, and ultimately enable activation-optimizing rehabilitation robot behavior, we present a personalizable transformer-based model mapping individuals' muscle activations (as measured via surface electromyography) to prescribed contact force trajectories when interacting with an end-effector rehabilitation robot. The model uses a transformer encoder-decoder leveraging rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to generate a latent representation of trajectory-relevant and user-specific neuromotor factors, and augments trajectory prediction with flow matching to produce a distribution over plausible prescriptions biased toward the training distribution. Using data from 16 healthy participants completing 15 isometric trajectory tracking tasks, we evaluate generalization across held-out tasks and users, as well as the feasibility of user-specific fine-tuning within a therapy-session timescale. The model achieves mean trajectory prediction errors of  < 8% on held out tasks and users, with effectively instantaneous deterministic inference and sub-second sampling of trajectory distributions. An initial test using the model during live rehabilitation tasks demonstrates that, on average, participants reach the target neuromotor activations with just 15% error accumulated throughout the task. These results provide a proof of concept for data-driven, activation-targeted trajectory prescription in robot-mediated rehabilitation and establish a foundation for future validation in clinical populations. Data and code have been open-sourced as part of the OpenRobotRehab project on SimTK.","title":"Transformer-Based Trajectory Prescription for sEMG-Optimizing Robot-Mediated Rehabilitation","title_en":"Transformer-Based Trajectory Prescription for sEMG-Optimizing Robot-Mediated Rehabilitation","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08295v1","version":"v1","version_updated_at":"2026-11-05T16:55:55Z"}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.08097","authors":["Youhao Lyu","Chenghao Sun","Zhenxuan Ding","Shuting Zhang","Ziyang Dong","Wenhao Cui"],"categories":["cs.RO"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08097"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-05T14:40:52Z","rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"For perceptive humanoid locomotion, the relevance of terrain geometry depends on the robot's body state and how both evolve under its actions. Existing work has advanced terrain-aware sensory fusion and cross-modal prediction, improving how visual and proprioceptive information is combined and related. However, feature aggregation alone does not specify which cross-modal relationships should be learned, while prediction between simultaneous observations does not explicitly constrain their action-dependent evolution. We present Spatiotemporal Training with Explicit Prediction (STEP), a one-stage framework that jointly supervises cross-modal relationships and action-dependent state evolution within a shared control representation. Multiple learned queries aggregate depth and proprioceptive tokens into a compact policy state. Bidirectional masked prediction uses each visible modality to predict latent features of the omitted modality, explicitly supervising terrain-body relationships. An action-conditioned predictor maps the current policy state and executed action to the next fused state, with an exponential-moving-average target defined directly in the policy representation space. Simulation comparisons show overall improvements in terrain traversal over evaluated fusion alternatives and ablations, while depth-dropout and delay experiments demonstrate the benefits of both predictive objectives under degraded visual input. Deployed on a 23-DoF Noetix E1 humanoid with onboard sensing, STEP succeeds in 98 of 100 hardware trials across stairs, a 40\\,cm platform, a 70\\,cm gap, stepping stones, and backward stair traversal without rearward terrain visibility.","title":"STEP: Spatiotemporal Training with Explicit Prediction for Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion","title_en":"STEP: Spatiotemporal Training with Explicit Prediction for Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08097v1","version":"v1","version_updated_at":"2026-11-05T14:40:52Z"}

{"arxiv_id":"2303.04137","authors":["Cheng Chi","Zhenjia Xu","Siyuan Feng","Eric Cousineau","Yilun Du","Benjamin Burchfiel","Russ Tedrake","Shuran Song"],"categories":["cs.RO"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2303.04137"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["diffusion_policy"],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2023-03-07T18:50:03Z","rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"This paper introduces Diffusion Policy, a new way of generating robot behavior by representing a robot's visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process. We benchmark Diffusion Policy across 12 different tasks from 4 different robot manipulation benchmarks and find that it consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art robot learning methods with an average improvement of 46.9%. Diffusion Policy learns the gradient of the action-distribution score function and iteratively optimizes with respect to this gradient field during inference via a series of stochastic Langevin dynamics steps. We find that the diffusion formulation yields powerful advantages when used for robot policies, including gracefully handling multimodal action distributions, being suitable for high-dimensional action spaces, and exhibiting impressive training stability. To fully unlock the potential of diffusion models for visuomotor policy learning on physical robots, this paper presents a set of key technical contributions including the incorporation of receding horizon control, visual conditioning, and the time-series diffusion transformer. We hope this work will help motivate a new generation of policy learning techniques that are able to leverage the powerful generative modeling capabilities of diffusion models. Code, data, and training details is publicly available diffusion-policy.cs.columbia.edu","title":"Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion","title_en":"Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04137v5","version":"v5","version_updated_at":"2024-03-14T04:36:31Z"}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.09877","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.09877"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.09877v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Tendon-driven continuum robots can reach through constrained spaces, but contact along their bodies is invisible to the sensors at their motors. We show that this is a structural limitation rather than a tuning problem: the map from contact forces to tendon measurements has a null space of dimension at least seven, so no estimator that leaves the contact support free can locate contact. When the obstacle geometry is known, however, non-penetration and complementarity make the contact force locally identifiable, and we prove that the resulting system with unknown contact inputs is locally exponentially strongly detectable. We present a constrained moving horizon estimator (MHE) that encodes these conditions and runs in real time as one quadratic program per sample, and we give a local, mode-wise robust stability result for it. In a finite- element benchmark of a two-section robot pressing and sliding on a wall, the estimator located contact to 0.9 mm and estimated contact force to 0.22 N, compared with 65 mm and 0.72 N for a tuned extended Kalman filter (EKF) with state projection. The estimator tolerated millimeter- level errors in the obstacle position and unmodeled wall friction, under which the projected EKF failed. Under randomized model mismatch over 40 trials, including unmodeled tendon friction, it remained better in force and location in every trial. Yet different coordinates can describe the same interaction, whereas similar motions can produce different outcomes when local physical conditions change. How these distinctions affect learned prediction remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates matched action representations defined in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark. Global pose and contact relocation experiments reveal a cost associated with limited training data when equivalent interactions receive different spatial descriptions. Removing information about peel thickness creates an irreducible ambiguity because identical predictive inputs can correspond to different material removal outcomes. Coordinates defined relative to the surface improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection under accurate local observations, but learned predictors remain vulnerable to uncertainty in the coordinate frame. Joint centering of the surface and tool removes sensitivity to translation of their common origin, whereas incorrect contact geometry and actual execution deviations introduce different failure mechanisms. These results show that effective spatial generalization depends on preserving the relationships between actions and states that determine physical consequences, rather than simply minimizing coordinate variation. This perspective provides a principled basis for designing robot world models that reuse physical knowledge across spatial configurations while retaining the distinctions essential to prediction and planning.","title":"Action Representation for Spatial Generalization in Robot World Models","title_en":"Action Representation for Spatial Generalization in Robot World Models","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11869","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2512.07976","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2512.07976"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["reinforcement_learning"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2512.07976v3 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: Training end-to-end policies from image data to directly predict navigation actions for robotic systems has proven inherently difficult. Existing approaches often suffer from either the sim-to-real gap during policy transfer or limited action-labeled training data. To address this problem, we introduce Visual Learned Distance (VLD), a scalable framework for image-goal navigation that decouples perception learning from policy learning. We first train a self-supervised distance-to-goal predictor on about 3,000 hours of internet-scale and simulated video, providing a distance signal that a reinforcement learning (RL) policy can minimize. The RL policy is trained separately in simulation using privileged geometric distances perturbed by GeoNoise, a learned noise model that reproduces the viewpoint- and overlap-dependent errors of the trained distance predictor. At deployment, the policy consumes VLD predictions zero-shot, without retraining, inheriting ``where to go'' from large-scale visual training while retaining the robust navigation behaviors learned in simulation. This error modeling is key to the transfer: with VLD inputs, GeoNoise-trained policies reach $58.7\\%$ success on HM3D and $76.2\\%$ on Gibson, whereas policies trained with generic temporally correlated noise collapse to $4.9\\%$ and $11.5\\%$. {"arxiv_id":"2611.09270","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.09270"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.09270v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Rough terrain traversability is often estimated through point-wise roll, pitch, or force-angle margins along a planned path. However, these metrics are often inaccurate and overly conservative because they ignore how terrain disturbances and low-level controller corrections can affect the vehicle's motions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT), defined as the probability that a vehicle-controller pair can execute a candidate path while meeting trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements. We estimate EGT by predicting the distribution of closed-loop trajectories using a latent-space flow matching (FM) model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features and 3D vehicle attitude and wheel-ground contact points prior. Across 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT reduces safe-path rejection to 2.2% (versus 11.4%-39.5% for pose-margin and force-angle baselines) and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%. Integrated into a receding-horizon sampling-based planner, EGT reduces navigation failure rates by 24-42 and 30-44 percentage points over [1] and [2], respectively, while cutting goal-reaching time by up to 20.5% and 45%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer of our simulation-trained model to real-world outdoor experiments.","title":"EGT: Execution-Grounded Traversability through Learned Closed-Loop Trajectory Distributions","title_en":"EGT: Execution-Grounded Traversability through Learned Closed-Loop Trajectory Distributions","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09270","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.12136","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.12136"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.12136v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: We study humanoid navigation across multiple destinations under long-horizon language instructions. This task is challenging because robots must maintain progress across successive goals while continuously producing natural, stable whole-body motion through confined spaces. However, task decomposition in existing methods does not by itself ensure progress throughout execution, while waypoint-based navigation does not guarantee natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. Our key idea is to organize navigation into three complementary roles operating at different time scales: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body execution. We realize this idea in LHNav, an asynchronous system that uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and whole-body control. To train the Cerebellum for natural, route-faithful motion, we develop a physics-grounded data engine that improves physical tracking of motion references along collision-aware routes and pairs the resulting demonstrations with rendered visual observations. Together, these designs allow task planning to proceed alongside continuous movement and extend single-goal navigation to successive destinations with natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. In simulation, our navigation VLA outperforms OmniNav and DualVLN in single-goal success and motion smoothness, with fewer collisions and falls. Using a VLA trained only on single-goal demonstrations, LHNav achieves a 75.56% success rate on long-horizon navigation tasks. {"arxiv_id":"2611.10343","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.10343"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.10343v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Generative robot policies based on diffusion and flow matching can model complex, multimodal behaviors, but remain susceptible to covariate shift during closed-loop execution. Existing approaches mitigate such failures through additional demonstrations, policy fine-tuning, or test-time guidance, but often require human intervention, engineered rewards, or other task-specific signals. We introduce GUARD, an anomaly-informed Q-steering framework that leverages the policy's training distribution to construct a dense, failure-anticipatory steering signal. GUARD pairs sparse task rewards with dense anomaly scores learned from policy training data and propagates both through a learned Q-function. Its gradients then steer the denoising process toward actions that improve task return while preventing trajectories from entering poorly supported regions, without directly modifying the pretrained policy. Across four Adroit dexterous manipulation tasks, GUARD achieves average success rates of $96.0\\%$ and $80.0\\%$ under nominal and perturbed dynamics, outperforming the strongest baseline by $21.0$ and $20.0$ percentage points while maintaining the lowest anomaly score. GUARD further demonstrates direct sim-to-real transfer on in-hand screwdriver rotation and reorientation tasks, achieving $40$ and $25$ percentage-point gains in success rate. These results demonstrate that anomaly signals can serve not only for failure monitoring but also to complement sparse task rewards as effective supervision for robust policy steering.","title":"GUARD: Anomaly-Informed Q-Steering for Generative Robot Policies in Dexterous Manipulation","title_en":"GUARD: Anomaly-Informed Q-Steering for Generative Robot Policies in Dexterous Manipulation","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10343","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.08373","authors":["Fuhao Li","Wenxuan Song","Qizhou Huang","Ziyang Zhou","Jingbo Wang","Junwu E","Pengwei Wang","Yan Wang","Shunbo Zhou","Haoang Li"],"categories":["cs.RO"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08373"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["vla"],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-05T17:52:16Z","rule_score":90,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.","title":"SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training","title_en":"SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08373v1","version":"v1","version_updated_at":"2026-11-05T17:52:16Z"}

{"arxiv_id":"2606.18634","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2606.18634"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2606.18634v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: To locate a target object while exploring the unknown environment is a fundamental capability for autonomous agents, with applications ranging from search-and-rescue to field robots. A simplified version of such task is Object Goal Navigation (ObjNav). In ObjNav, successful arrival at the target object provides a basic measure of performance; however, the efficiency of the navigation trajectory is equally important, as it indicates how intelligently the agent explores and how much time remains for subsequent tasks. In unknown environments, the key to efficient navigation lies in deciding where to explore next. While many prior works aim to address this core challenge and achieved promising performance in certain settings, recent training-based models and non-training frameworks still suffer from generalization and efficiency issues respectively, which in the worst cases can lead to excessive exploration of already-visited areas or redundant back-and-forth motion. We evaluate EffiNav on two widely used simulation benchmarks Habitat Matterport 3D (HM3D) and Open-Vocabulary Object goal Navigation (OVON), and further validate its effectiveness on physical robots in real-world settings. We conduct failure analysis on massive simulation episodes. With minimal modification, we also extend EffiNav to a memory-augmented ObjNav task on the GOAT-BENCH dataset, demonstrating its adaptability beyond standard ObjNav settings. Across two standard metrics--Success Rate (SR) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), EffiNav matches or outperforms recent baselines, reflecting its efficiency, robustness, and practical applicability. Recognizing the different emphases of the two datasets, the performances reveals this framework is more balanced and generalizable for efficient ObjNav.","title":"EffiNav: Fusing Depth and Vision-Language for Efficient Object Goal Navigation","title_en":"EffiNav: Fusing Depth and Vision-Language for Efficient Object Goal Navigation","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18634","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.11605","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.11605"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.11605v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Quadrotors inspecting buildings and tunnels must navigate unknown clutter with a forward-facing depth camera whose limited field of view constrains scene understanding and collision-avoiding navigation. Recent world-model agents learn navigation through imagined experience (e.g., AirDreamer), but remain data-intensive and often lack explicit geometric memory and awareness of what the camera can observe. We propose ScanDreamer, a map-grounded world model that constructs an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose. Our world model, actor, and critic are conditioned on this map, which also defines a geodesic progress reward. Moreover, a forward-cone penalty discourages horizontal motion outside the camera's viewing direction. During imagination, ScanDreamer propagates the quadrotor pose over a frozen map and derives progress and wall-contact signals from the mapped geometry. We train ScanDreamer for 0.8 million environment steps (5.5 h on one GPU) and evaluate it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim over 1560 episodes spanning unseen layouts and parameter ranges. Removing the forward-cone penalty increases collisions to 9.9 $\\pm$ 3.1%. These results show that combining explicit map memory, map-grounded imagination, and perception-aware motion substantially improves navigation performance and data efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/WANGSHUAIzzzz/ScanDreamer.","title":"ScanDreamer: A Map-Grounded World Model for Quadrotor Navigation","title_en":"ScanDreamer: A Map-Grounded World Model for Quadrotor Navigation","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11605","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. {"arxiv_id":"2412.01753","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2412.01753"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2412.01753v3 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: This review explores the evolution of human-machine interfaces (HMIs) in subsea telerobotics, charting the progression from traditional first-person \"soda-straw\" consoles-- characterized by narrow field-of-view camera feeds-- to contemporary interfaces leveraging gesture recognition, virtual reality, and natural language processing. The review makes three key contributions. First, we introduce a structured framework that analyzes subsea HMIs through three interrelated aspects: operator experience, robotic autonomy, and bidirectional human-machine communication. Second, using these aspects, we compare visual, haptic, extended-reality, gesture, and natural-language interfaces; examine the progression from direct teleoperation to shared autonomy; and assess the distinct roles of simulators and digital twins in training, prototyping, and mission support. Third, we synthesize the reported evidence to distinguish established industrial tools, selectively deployed technologies, and research-stage capabilities, while identifying limitations in interoperability, communication reliability, immersive feedback, and field validation. From this synthesis, we outline standardization needs and research directions for hydrodynamic feedback, latency-aware shared autonomy, grounded language interaction, and real-to-simulation transfer. {"arxiv_id":"2611.10435","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.10435"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":50,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.10435v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Autonomous robot teams deployed in remote, unstructured environments may face changes in the environment, hardware, and team composition that degrade previously effective policies. Shifting mission objectives can be handled by selecting a different solution from an existing Pareto set, but shifting deployment conditions can reorder the set itself, making previously dominated policies competitive or new policies necessary. However, evaluating these policies in new contexts while minimizing risk to the hardware remains an open problem. We argue that, although largely untested in this domain, world models merit investigation for post-deployment multi-objective adaptation. This paper presents Agibot, an open-source, modular, low-cost agricultural robotics platform designed for autonomy research and experimentation, with potential applications in hands-on robotics education. The platform integrates four-wheel independent swerve drive, swappable computing, distributed embedded control, multimodal sensing, and configurable manipulation within a unified sense-plan-act-verify framework supporting perception, control, navigation, manipulation, and autonomous task verification. The platform was evaluated through representative row-crop navigation and manipulation tasks under varying lighting and soil conditions. Experiments demonstrated reliable lane following, autonomous row-to-row navigation, target identification, seed dispensing, plant manipulation, and closed-loop verification of task success. Its modular architecture supports independent testing, modification, and validation of autonomy components for rapid prototyping and experimentation. These proof-of-concept tasks, controller-tuning studies, and integrated trials demonstrate the platform's research capabilities, while its accessible and reconfigurable design supports its use for hands-on robotics education. {"arxiv_id":"2611.11438","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.11438"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.11438v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.","title":"When Coding Agents Get Arms: Safety Risks Across the Digital-Physical Boundary","title_en":"When Coding Agents Get Arms: Safety Risks Across the Digital-Physical Boundary","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11438","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.09266","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.09266"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["reinforcement_learning"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.09266v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Scaling up visual humanoid loco-manipulation skill acquisition requires reducing the human effort needed as tasks and spatial configurations expand, particularly in demonstration collection and task-specific training design. We present SUGARv2, a unified framework for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills through interaction reference synthesis and a shared training pipeline. To obtain diverse references at low cost, we adapt reusable task templates to different spatial configurations, synthesizing coordinated robot and object motions. To reduce task-specific reward design and training effort, we use reference-based imitation as a common learning objective across tasks. We first train privileged teachers to execute these references, then train visual policies through teacher distillation and reinforcement learning with the same reference-based mimic rewards, using diverse object instances and visual domain randomization to support visual generalization and sim-to-real transfer. Across five humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, SUGARv2 achieves a mean success rate of 91.0% in simulation. {"arxiv_id":"2611.12120","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.12120"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":40,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.12120v1 Announce Type: cross \nAbstract: Autonomous agents must continually acquire reusable knowledge from experience without relying on costly large language model (LLM) reasoning for every decision. However, existing experience-based approaches often struggle to transform accumulated observations and reasoning into compact knowledge that lightweight models can independently apply. This paper proposes SCALE, a small-model-first framework that integrates selective LLM reasoning, experience-driven concept abstraction, and knowledge internalization. A lightweight model handles routine predictions, while prediction errors and accumulated cross-episode evidence selectively trigger LLM reflection. The LLM analyzes relevant historical experiences, generates positive and negative counterfactual examples, and proposes reusable concept hypotheses. Independently validated concepts are progressively incorporated into hierarchical neural representations, enabling lightweight models to exploit increasingly abstract knowledge. Meanwhile, mastered experiences are excluded from active memory while their original records remain available in a complete archive. {"arxiv_id":"2611.10967","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.10967"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.10967v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Dexterous manipulation with world action models (WAMs) relies on hand configuration and contact information, yet joint-state and whole-hand tactile observations may be partially or entirely missing. RGB images provide scene context and hand-object geometry but are insufficient to reliably recover these missing modalities. We further observe a correlation between hand state and tactile information. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BAT-WAM, a framework that bridges visual, joint-state, and tactile representations for WAMs. BAT-WAM learns separate codebooks and decoders for the tactile and action streams. An RGB-conditioned continuous latent bridge connects the two streams for bidirectional learning, while visual information serves as continuous context. Under the HTBench evaluation protocol, BAT-WAM reduces the root mean squared error (RMSE) of tactile reconstruction by 34.73% under fully masked conditions and 38.84% under partially masked conditions, relative to an image-conditioned HandTouch checkpoint. For future tactile prediction conditioned on target-time RGB and historical actions, it reduces mean RMSE by 85.56% relative to OpenWAM with HandTouch. Real-robot experiments further show that BAT-WAM consistently outperforms related WAM baselines in dexterous manipulation. Generalization experiments on unseen objects and scenes also demonstrate substantial improvements over baseline models. These findings support joint modeling of visual context, hand state, and touch as a representation approach for multimodal WAMs.","title":"BAT-WAM: Bridging Action and Touch in World-Action Models for Dexterous Hands","title_en":"BAT-WAM: Bridging Action and Touch in World-Action Models for Dexterous Hands","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10967","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.09605","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.09605"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.09605v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Humanoid whole-body control requires a robot to track diverse reference motions while maintaining balance under gravity, torque limits, contact switching, and external disturbances. Existing reinforcement-learning-based trackers typically learn control outputs that jointly address motion tracking and balance. However, similar reference poses can correspond to substantially different dynamic demands, requiring a unified policy to learn motion-dependent control requirements alongside balance corrections. This can complicate learning and lead to high-frequency fluctuations in control outputs. We propose DKWBC, a dynamics-informed whole-body control framework that combines explicit model-based tracking with a learned balancing residual. Inspired by the model-based and environmental-wrench contributions to joint torques in floating-base dynamics, DKWBC uses inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint PD feedback to supply tracking torques, while a residual policy learns additional joint-torque corrections for balanced execution. By explicitly accounting for motion-dependent torque demands, this structure simplifies the policy's learning task. Experiments in simulation and on real hardware demonstrate that a single learned balancing policy generalizes across motion datasets while maintaining accurate motion tracking and balance across ground support, attached payloads, and physical interaction. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DKWBC/.","title":"DKWBC: Decoupling Motion Tracking and Balancing for Humanoid Whole-Body Control","title_en":"DKWBC: Decoupling Motion Tracking and Balancing for Humanoid Whole-Body Control","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09605","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.08364","authors":["Chang Shi","Ann Majewicz Fey"],"categories":["cs.RO","cs.LG"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08364"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["reinforcement_learning"],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-05T17:42:31Z","rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor--critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73\\% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03\\% vs. 0.63\\%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.","title":"SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing","title_en":"SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08364v1","version":"v1","version_updated_at":"2026-11-05T17:42:31Z"}

This paper investigates a radial basis function (RBF) neural network compensator whose output is shared by a Cartesian tracking controller and a joint-space CBF filter. An auxiliary state driven by the difference between requested and applied torques corrects the learning signal, reducing the direct influence of filter intervention on adaptation. A two-link manipulator is evaluated through constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbance trials, and operating-range and timing studies. {"arxiv_id":"2611.11697","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.11697"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["vla"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.11697v1 Announce Type: cross \nAbstract: Understanding 3D scene dynamics in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is a fundamental step toward physically intelligent and autonomous surgical systems. However, existing public datasets offer limited scalability and diversity in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, annotations typically focus on either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions. This gap limits applications such as augmented reality guidance and autonomous surgery driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models or world models, which demand large-scale, high-quality 3D supervision. In this work, we construct SurgTAP-3D, a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark, comprising 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from diverse robotic and manual procedures under unified action categories. To make annotation scalable, we design a unified framework for surgical 3D point tracking that converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement. This pipeline adapts foundation priors to surgical videos and produces temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks. The dataset captures realistic challenges inherent to surgical environments, including occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and rapid instrument motion. We establish a comprehensive benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT, and STIR, covering both instrument and tissue tracking. We demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and annotation framework for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding. Learned subgoal policies can guide model predictive control beyond its local prediction horizon, but a geometrically suitable subgoal does not necessarily lead to a successfully solved control problem. This paper proposes OASIS, a hierarchical navigation framework that incorporates recent optimization outcomes into reinforcement learning-based subgoal generation. A high-level policy trained using Soft Actor--Critic generates local subgoals, while a nonlinear model predictive controller tracks them subject to motion limits, geometric collision-avoidance constraints, and embedded high-order control barrier function constraints. The outcomes of controller optimizations over each subgoal interval are summarized and provided to the policy at its next decision, without requiring additional optimization calls. The framework is evaluated in five navigation scenarios with static and moving obstacles, including dense interactions and sensing uncertainty. Comparisons with hierarchical and direct-goal control variants show that OASIS achieves the highest aggregate navigation success. Matched comparisons across three training seeds further show a consistent success advantage over the otherwise identical hierarchy without optimization-status input. {"arxiv_id":"2611.10366","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.10366"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.10366v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Directing a robot to locate a target object in unseen environments remains a central challenge in embodied AI. Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based methods provide rich semantic reasoning but often produce uncalibrated and overconfident action decisions. We introduce CPNav, a navigation framework that combines collision-aware planning with statistically calibrated VLM action scoring for map-free object-goal navigation. From RGB-D input, CPNav constructs a navigability map, generates collision-free motion primitives, and queries two VLMs for goal detection and action scoring. The resulting scores are calibrated offline via conformal prediction (CP) using oracle actions obtained through a tree-structured exploration procedure with backtracking, providing finite-sample guarantees at a user-specified risk level. The CP layer is model-agnostic and can wrap any VLM policy. Online, calibrated VLM scores guide action selection, while a tree-structured exploration history records alternative actions and allows backtracking. We evaluate CPNav in both simulation and real-world hardware settings. In AI Habitat simulation, compared with the uncalibrated baseline method, CPNav achieves relative SR and SPL improvements of 6.2% and 11.4% on HM3D v0.2, and 12.4% and 8.8% on MP3D, respectively. In real-world deployment on a modified Hiwonder MentorPi robot, the corresponding improvements in SR and SPL are 24.9% and 15.2%, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/practice-lab-ucla/CPnav.","title":"CPNav: Calibrated Vision-Language Navigation for Object-Goal Search in Unseen Environments","title_en":"CPNav: Calibrated Vision-Language Navigation for Object-Goal Search in Unseen Environments","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10366","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.12251","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.12251"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["reinforcement_learning","imitation_learning"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.12251v1 Announce Type: cross \nAbstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from raw sensory inputs such as images or onboard sensors can be challenging due to high-dimensional observations and sparse rewards. A common strategy is to train a teacher policy with access to privileged state information and then distill it into a student policy that acts from raw inputs alone. However, when the teacher relies on information unavailable to the student, exact imitation may be impossible, creating an irreducible imitation gap. Existing approaches typically mitigate this mismatch through careful reward shaping or additional reinforcement learning on the student policy after the teacher has been trained. Instead, we introduce Representation-Aligned Imitation Learning (RAIL), which addresses the mismatch during teacher training itself. RAIL learns a latent representation shared across teacher and student observations using contrastive learning, and trains the teacher policy directly in this space. Because the teacher policy is constrained to operate on this shared space, it learns behaviors that are reproducible from student observations. This substantially reduces the imitation gap while preserving task performance. Across multiple environments, RAIL outperforms strong baselines without reward modification or post-hoc student fine-tuning, and surpasses direct reinforcement learning from raw observations. The learned representations further enable zero-shot transfer to new tasks through teacher-only training. Guidewires reach deep into the ducts but are blind, whereas cholangioscopes provide vision but are too large to readily enter the pancreatic body and tail, the cystic duct, or the gallbladder. At the millimeter scale of these ducts, every function added to a steerable catheter competes with steering for cross-section and adds bending stiffness. We present a 1.47-mm modular magnetic soft robotic catheter in which each function is built into the magnetic body, onto its surface, or onto the footprint of the camera, and we measured what each function costs in bending under bedside fields. Imaging and fiber Bragg grating (FBG) shape sensing accounted for most of this cost, whereas a compliant gripper, magnetic anchoring balloons, and a micrometer-thick ultrasound-triggered release shell together reduced the tip angle at 8 mT only from 70{\\deg} to 64{\\deg}. In live pigs, the robotic catheter performed operator-initiated task-autonomous cannulation of the native papilla without sphincterotomy and was teleoperated under onboard vision 75 mm into the pancreatic duct and, without a guidewire, through the cystic duct into the gallbladder, whose lumen it imaged. {"arxiv_id":"2611.08920","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08920"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.08920v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Human videos contain abundant object-manipulation demonstrations, but they do not directly provide motion cues that a robot can follow. We present HOC2R, a Hand-Object Contact trajectory extractor for Robot motion that combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand-object association and contact localization. HOC2R supports two modes: count-aware automation that detects, counts, and localizes visible contacts in untrimmed videos, and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers when contact frames are known. On a 30-task point-annotated benchmark, count-aware automation improves contact-count accuracy from 58.1% to 71.4% and reduces mean localization distance from 19.81 to 10.46 pixels relative to an adapted VRB2 baseline. On seven unseen RGB-D rollouts, a five-task fixed-two checkpoint reduces mean localization distance from 67.67 to 27.02 pixels. Across six robot evaluation sequences, the 30-task fixed-two checkpoint produces four feasible trajectories and succeeds on three tasks, compared with two feasible trajectories and one successful task for each adapted baseline. HOC2R is competitive in the evaluated single-hand scenes, robust to the hand-color shift, and strongest in the evaluated multi-hand scenes. These results support HOC2R as a practical pseudo-labeling method for extracting robot-usable contact trajectories from human demonstrations.","title":"HOC2R: Hand-Object Contact Trajectories for Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer","title_en":"HOC2R: Hand-Object Contact Trajectories for Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08920","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.10510","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.10510"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.10510v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Self-improvement on compositional manipulation tasks requires deciding what to reuse, where to improve, and which changes to retain. We present ReSkill, a selective self-improvement framework that concentrates revision on capability gaps. A coding agent constructs an object-centric task graph from an instruction and a skill library, then uses node-level execution records to locate failures. At the task level, it revises stage organization, hand-off conditions, and recovery routes; at the skill level, it strengthens perception, motion, manipulation, and verification capabilities that repeatedly fail. Candidate revisions undergo full-task evaluation and paired comparisons before adoption, allowing local changes to accumulate into validated skills and an independently executable policy. The agent participates only during development; the deployed policy calls the retained skills without invoking the agent at run time. On the same development set, average success across ten RoboDojo tasks rises from 30.0% for the initial versions to 86.2% for the final adopted programs; retained programs achieve 83.6% in recorded robustness and model-selection evaluations. Across eight real-world tasks, ReSkill succeeds in 72 of 80 rebuilt-simulation trials and 62 of 80 real-robot trials (77.5%). The median revision changes only three functions, approximately 0.5% of a program, while 39% of task-specific functions in later-added tasks directly reuse existing implementations. These results show how locating local deficiencies, validating candidate changes, and accumulating reusable skills can improve execution of compositional manipulation tasks.","title":"ReSkill: Selective Self-Improvement for Robot Manipulation","title_en":"ReSkill: Selective Self-Improvement for Robot Manipulation","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10510","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.12306","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.12306"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.12306v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Wearable robots depend on a software chain that links body-worn sensing to gait interpretation, assistance generation, and actuation. Personalization further requires each measured response to remain associated with the assistance parameters that generated it. This paper presents ExoStack, a modular ROS 2 framework for implementing that chain across embedded hubs and a host computer. Its Embedded Sensing and Actuation (ESA) library configures ESP32 boards as microROS sensing and actuation hubs. ExoCore supplies multi-hub synchronization, gait-event detection, profile generation, motion planning, cost evaluation, and human-in-the-loop (HIL) optimization as configuration-instantiated nodes. The PASE desktop application edits configurations, launches the processing stages, and visualizes ROS 2 topics. Hardware drivers and algorithm plugins can be added through defined interfaces without modifying the generic processing nodes. We characterize hub and planner timing on three embedded computers and demonstrate reuse on two pneumatic exosuits.","title":"ExoStack: A Modular and Reconfigurable Software Framework for Wearable Robotics Using ROS 2","title_en":"ExoStack: A Modular and Reconfigurable Software Framework for Wearable Robotics Using ROS 2","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12306","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

Although flipping is a common objective in industrial tasks such as parts inspection, mechanical assembly, and tool use, coding a bimanual robot with grippers to flip diverse objects is a significant challenge. In this paper, we show that a coding agent can autonomously develop and refine object-flipping strategies through iterative learning in physics simulations across diverse object geometries. Progressive skill acquisition, from basic handover to toppling and pushing, robust grasping and sensing, and thin-object manipulation with recovery, improves task success from 24.7% to 95.0%. The resulting graph-based code integrates high-level strategy selection with reactive control, enabling multi-stage flipping on physical robots.","title":"Flip Anything with Agentic Robotics Self-Learning","title_en":"Flip Anything with Agentic Robotics Self-Learning","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11941","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

However, a fundamental spectral mismatch often exists between the high-rank transition dynamics of continuous environments and the low-rank bottleneck of the FB architecture, making accurate low-rank representation learning difficult. In this work, we analyze temporal abstraction as a mechanism to mitigate this mismatch. By characterizing the spectral properties of the transition operator, we show that temporal abstraction acts analogously to a low-pass filter that suppresses high-frequency spectral components. {"arxiv_id":"2607.04689","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2607.04689"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2607.04689v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: Reliable temporal representation learning is important for end-to-end autonomous driving, particularly when visual observations are degraded by occlusion, motion blur, illumination variation, and sensor noise. Existing Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) approaches provide a unified representation for perception and planning; however, temporal features are commonly aggregated across frames without explicitly accounting for the reliability of individual observations. Consequently, low-quality or inconsistent features may propagate through temporal representations and degrade downstream perception, prediction, and planning. To address this problem, we propose RCT-AD, a Reliability-Aware Context and Temporal BEV Reasoning framework for end-to-end autonomous driving that explicitly models feature reliability and temporal consistency within a shared BEV representation. RCT-AD introduces a Reliable Context Awareness (RCA) module that estimates frame-level reliability using spatial, semantic, temporal, and visual-quality cues, and selectively preserves trustworthy information through a reliability-guided temporal memory mechanism. When the current observation is unreliable, historical high-reliability features are aligned and integrated to construct a more stable temporal BEV representation. A Temporal Trajectory Planner models long-term temporal dependencies and multi-agent interactions, while semantic segmentation and motion-guided detection provide complementary supervision for refining the shared BEV representation. Experiments on the nuScenes benchmark demonstrate consistent improvements across perception, motion prediction, and trajectory planning. RCT-AD achieves 61.5 NDS, 52.9 mAP, and 52.3 mIoU while maintaining competitive computational efficiency. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of reliability-aware temporal BEV reasoning for unified perception, prediction, and planning.","title":"RCT-AD: Reliability-Aware Context and Temporal BEV Reasoning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving","title_en":"RCT-AD: Reliability-Aware Context and Temporal BEV Reasoning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04689","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.11868","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.11868"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["reinforcement_learning"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.11868v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Exploration in deep reinforcement learning (RL) for continuous control is commonly driven by temporally uncorrelated Gaussian (white) action noise, which leads to jerky motions with locally constrained exploration. In contrast, temporally correlated coloured noise, particularly pink noise, has been shown to support more efficient exploration in RL. Motivated by these findings, we inquire whether scheduling changes to the noise colour over the course of training can outperform white noise for continuous control robotics. We perform a systematic study of 49 linear schedules between white and red noise, together with generalised state-dependent exploration (gSDE), on four sparse-reward manipulation tasks with a Fetch arm and a Shadow Dexterous Hand. We find that the noise colour at the end of training does not affect learning efficiency or end performance, whereas fading towards red noise halves the jerk of exploration in every task. Balancing learning efficiency, end performance and smoothness, red noise emerges as the preferred strategy: it learns as efficiently as pink noise with almost 2-fold less movement jerk. We therefore recommend exploration schedulers that fade towards red noise as the default for off-policy robot learning.","title":"Fade to... Red? Scheduling Coloured Noise Exploration Supports Efficient Robot Learning with Reduced Movement Jerk","title_en":"Fade to... Red? We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge. By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer. On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks. Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%. These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching. WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision. Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.","title":"WorldBridge: Bridging Video and Action for Task Generalization in World Action Models","title_en":"WorldBridge: Bridging Video and Action for Task Generalization in World Action Models","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40748","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.11732","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.11732"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.11732v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Generative models can support both state estimation and control in robotics. For control, a common approach is to use the model as a policy that directly samples actions conditioned on observation histories. However, models that jointly represent states, actions, and observations can also predict how the robot state and its environment evolve. We investigate whether these predictions can improve state estimation and control through a change in inference procedure, without modifying the pretrained model. To this end, we use particle filtering to maintain competing hypotheses about state histories. A single pretrained diffusion model generates these hypotheses along with their predicted observations and associated action proposals. As new measurements arrive, particles are reweighted according to how well their predicted observations match the measurements. While particle filtering conventionally uses these weights only for state estimation, we also use them to guide action selection, favoring proposals associated with hypotheses that better explain the observations. Simulation experiments in partially observed navigation and vision-based manipulation demonstrate improvements in both state estimation and task performance compared to action generation without filtering, using the same pretrained model and no additional test-time information.","title":"Particle Filtering with Generative Trajectory Models for State Estimation and Control","title_en":"Particle Filtering with Generative Trajectory Models for State Estimation and Control","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11732","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.13114","authors":["Erik Derner","Jiří Kubalík","Robert Babuška"],"categories":["cs.RO","cs.AI","cs.CL","cs.LG","eess.SY"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.13114"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-09T19:03:05Z","rule_score":50,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"System identification requires expert decisions on the identification method, incorporation of prior physical knowledge, and model validation. We propose ASPIRE, a framework for nonlinear system identification in which a large language model agent selects and executes the identification method. ASPIRE constructs closed-form, nonlinear static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the intended use of the model, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. Each model includes its parameters, an estimation record, an interpretation of its terms, and an error evaluated on test data inaccessible to the agent. Formal physical requirements are verified independently. ASPIRE operates autonomously or interactively, allowing the agent to ask questions and the user to request further analyses and identification rounds. We evaluate ASPIRE on three measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Each system is tested with and without a description, in five runs per task. All 30 runs delivered valid models, at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run. An assessment by the authors found that, for the 30 models recommended by the agent, one per run, the interpretation of the model and the documentation of its structure selection and parameter estimation fully satisfied 132 of 150 assessed items and partly satisfied 18. {"arxiv_id":"2608.07555","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2608.07555"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":40,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2608.07555v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: Coding agents close the software loop for training a robot policy without having a human in the loop: a main agent manages the training, subagents analyze and execute, treat robot policies and hardware as tools and do the work. We port this architecture to robot-policy improvement, where one difference dominates the design: robotic tools such as trained policies, training pipelines, and data collection fail routinely, so a tool's quality must be measured, recorded at every call, and expired when the artifact behind it changes. AgenticRobotics is a backend-independent control plane in which an LLM controller drives disposable workers through durable train--evaluate--improve transactions: an immutable objective, controller-owned measurement, commit-keyed crash recovery, an evidence-graded skill library, and a tool registry with a standardized, recorded call surface.
