{"arxiv_id":"2611.11554","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.11554"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["vla"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.11554v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. {"arxiv_id":"2611.08914","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08914"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.08914v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.","title":"HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety","title_en":"HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08914","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2606.17241","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2606.17241"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2606.17241v2 Announce Type: replace-cross \nAbstract: Traffic sign recognition (TSR) systems deployed on embedded vehicular hardware face deployment effects that image-based benchmark evaluation does not capture, including frame-to-frame prediction instability in streaming video and load-dependent throughput under sustained operation. We present Edge-TSR, a continuous edge inference system for TSR on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano that combines sparse detection, multi-object tracking, region-level fine-grained classification, and a lightweight track-aware temporal stabilization mechanism adding only 0.07~ms per sampled frame. Evaluating on the source videos of the INTSD benchmark, we find that the state-of-the-art TSR models lose 20-30 percentage points of mAP@50 when moving from image-based to streaming evaluation. Edge-TSR achieves the best streaming classification performance among all evaluated baselines, and temporal stabilization improves accuracy by 10.58 percentage points over per-frame inference. We characterize latency, throughput, and thermal behavior across sampling intervals and four driving conditions, showing that throughput is load-proportional (20 ms per classified region) and that every-frame inference is limited by throughput rather than thermal throttling. A 55-minute, 26 km vehicular deployment demonstrates sustained online operation at 16.18 FPS within safe thermal limits without cloud offload. {"arxiv_id":"2611.11690","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.11690"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":40,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.11690v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate laboratory robotics and automation with AI-driven decision-making to close the design-build-test-learn (DBTL) cycle. However, physical testbeds that combine off-the-shelf hardware and AI into a functioning closed-loop workflow remain in early stages of development, and their integration with commercial laboratory automation is comparatively less developed. In this work, we develop a physical testbed that assembles and integrates commercially available laboratory automation instruments and demonstrate continuous, closed-loop, autonomous operation over 24 cumulative hours of unattended experimentation. We validate this platform on a minimal closed-loop discovery task in which the system autonomously formulates aqueous dye mixtures to match a target absorbance spectrum. The system completed six independent campaigns, each consisting of 48 closed-loop iterations over approximately four hours. In every campaign, the system autonomously selected, dispensed, and measured each mixture, with an AI-driven decision-making algorithm determining subsequent formulations without human intervention. Using this testbed, we compared the performance of two AI-driven decision-making algorithms, traditional Bayesian optimization (BO) and an agentic approach, in selecting mixtures under a fixed total-volume constraint. The agentic optimizer matched target absorbance spectra using fewer iterations than BO, with reductions up to 52%, and converged on a solution for one target that BO failed to match within 48 iterations. These results demonstrate a reference physical platform for SDLs that can evaluate both established and emerging AI strategies, including large language model (LLM)-directed optimization, before their deployment in real-world applications where experiments may be costly and time-consuming to prepare.","title":"A Physical Testbed for Self-Driving Laboratories: Comparing Bayesian and Agentic Optimization in a Minimal Closed-Loop Color Formulation Task","title_en":"A Physical Testbed for Self-Driving Laboratories: Comparing Bayesian and Agentic Optimization in a Minimal Closed-Loop Color Formulation Task","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11690","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.12175","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.12175"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.12175v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at https://github.com/Notfound-JH/GEOMIND-benchmark.git.","title":"GeoMind: A Benchmark for Spatial Understanding in Robotic Manipulation","title_en":"GeoMind: A Benchmark for Spatial Understanding in Robotic Manipulation","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12175","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.09937","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.09937"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["reinforcement_learning"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.09937v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Differentiable model predictive control (MPC) enables structured, constraint-aware policies to be optimized end-to-end. However, learning MPC policies faces two bottlenecks: (1) nonsmooth sensitivities at active-set transitions and (2) expensive policy evaluation, since each requires an optimization solve. We first introduce SmoothedTurboMPC, a GPU-parallel differentiable MPC solver combining sequential quadratic programming (SQP) with a log-barrier-smoothed alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) inner solver. Its design enables smooth gradients, exact sensitivities at convergence, and efficient execution on GPUs. Second, to efficiently train MPC policies, we pair our solver with first-order reinforcement learning (FORL) using Short-Horizon Actor-Critic (SHAC), which reuses rollout MPC solutions instead of repeatedly re-evaluating them. Comparisons with state of the art solvers show that the approach achieves up to $4.4\\times$ higher end-to-end training throughput. On a vehicle racing task, our method achieves higher returns than MPC PPO with a $46\\times$ speedup, training on 3.3 million transitions in only 7 minutes. Finally, we use the framework to train a more reliable MPC racing policy via RL with domain randomization, and validate it on a full-scale race car. We integrate our advances into the open-source TurboMPC solver.","title":"Efficient Learning of Differentiable MPC Policies on the GPU via Smoothed ADMM and First-Order Reinforcement Learning","title_en":"Efficient Learning of Differentiable MPC Policies on the GPU via Smoothed ADMM and First-Order Reinforcement Learning","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09937","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2604.22235","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2604.22235"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":50,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2604.22235v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: Industrial robots are widely used in manufacturing, yet most manipulation still depends on fixed waypoint scripts that are brittle to environmental changes. Learning-based control offers a more adaptive alternative, but it remains unclear whether such methods, still mostly confined to laboratory demonstrations, can sustain hours of reliable operation, deliver consistent quality, and behave safely around people on a live production line. Here we present Learning-Augmented Robotic Automation, a hybrid system that integrates learned task controllers and a neural 3D safety monitor into conventional industrial workflows. It retains the core industrial automation backbone while introducing learning only where adaptability is needed. We deployed the system on an electric-motor production line to automate deformable cable insertion and soldering under real manufacturing constraints, a step previously performed manually by human workers. With less than 20 minutes of real-world data per task, the system operated continuously for 5 hours 10 minutes, producing 108 motors without physical fencing and achieving a 99.4% pass rate on product-level quality-control tests. It achieved near-human takt time with reduced cycle-time variability while consistently producing high-quality solder joints comparable to those of experienced operators. These results establish a practical pathway for extending industrial automation with learning-based methods.","title":"Learning-augmented robotic automation for real-world manufacturing","title_en":"Learning-augmented robotic automation for real-world manufacturing","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22235","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.10241","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.10241"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.10241v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction turns an uncalibrated monocular stream into a dense point cloud in a single inference pass, orders of magnitude faster than classical structure-from-motion (e.g., COLMAP), and reliable on the weakly textured, repetitive surfaces where keypoint matching fails outright. However, raw point clouds lack the object identity, physical properties, and watertight volume required for robot learning. This gap widens under robot-native capture. A camera mounted on a robot constrained to a few degrees of freedom sees each object only partially, and the repetitive, weakly textured structure of an office makes distinct workstations nearly indistinguishable, leaving redundant and partial observations that downstream reconstruction cannot resolve. Existing image-to-3D generation methods struggle with these conditions, hallucinating geometry under incomplete views and confusing repeated instances. We present OfficeTwin, a robot-native framework that converts these incomplete observations into simulation-ready digital twins. OfficeTwin first imposes metric and structural constraints, then exploits the office's structural redundancy by registering repeated cubicles into a shared canonical frame, where complementary observations recover geometry occluded in any single view without hallucination. On a real office scan, OfficeTwin recovers every cubicle as an individually watertight, metric solid, outperforming feed-forward reconstruction and generative baselines that fail to produce simulation-ready assets.","title":"OfficeTwin: Realizing 3D Reconstruction of Redundant Scenes through Partial Viewpoint Perception","title_en":"OfficeTwin: Realizing 3D Reconstruction of Redundant Scenes through Partial Viewpoint Perception","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10241","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.09130","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.09130"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.09130v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Grasp-feasibility predictors report near-perfect accuracy on Task and Motion Planning benchmarks, but high accuracy on these benchmarks does not verify that a predictor uses the collision geometry that the motion planner checks. We propose a planner-verified counterfactual (CF) test: holding the grasp pose fixed, we insert a solid obstacle into the approach corridor, add its points to the model input, and let a planner re-derive the label, which flips from feasible to infeasible. Across eight predictors spanning point clouds, voxels, depth, and object tokens, CF-pair AUROC falls from high natural AUROC (0.920-0.996) to chance (0.470-0.504), and the flip holds across four planners, two arms, and a real-object obstacle. Predictors fail at different resolutions, from a bounding box to a 12.5 cm voxel. In the point-cloud models we dissect, the obstacle either moves the representation in a direction unrelated to whether it blocks the grasp or is not registered at all. {"arxiv_id":"2611.09888","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.09888"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":50,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.09888v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Scenario-based simulation is central to evaluating autonomous-driving policies, but a scenario scripted before execution (i.e., with predetermined, fixed actor routes and speeds) may not preserve its intended interaction once the tested ego policy responds in closed loop. Scripted scenarios cannot adapt to unanticipated ego behavior, while learned traffic actors may remain reactive without reliably realizing a particular scenario intent. We introduce a scenario orchestrator that continuously monitors the joint traffic state and adapts non-ego actors through re-timing, re-routing, and role reassignment for creating a specific scenario intent. At each step, the orchestrator solves a constrained optimization problem that preserves the intended interaction while limiting interventions and maintaining traffic feasibility. We further distinguish scenario realization from policy failure, allowing a test to first be judged based on whether the intended interaction occurred and then by how the ego policy responded. Experiments in the CARLA simulator across multiple scenario families and driving policies show that orchestration realizes targeted interactions more reliably than scripted and learned actor-level baselines, particularly under variations in initial conditions and ego behavior. {"arxiv_id":"2610.30320","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2610.30320"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2610.30320v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.","title":"Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models","title_en":"Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30320","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

## ⚠️ Breaking changes (v0.5.1 -> v0.6.0)

v0.6.0 cleans house, and a few changes need your attention when upgrading:

- `pip install lerobot` no longer includes dataset or training dependencies; add the extra you need (e.g. `lerobot[training]`).
- Some import paths have changed. Please use the canonical public entry points rather than internal submodule paths.
- GR00T N1.5 is replaced by N1.7 (pin `lerobot==0.5.1` if you need N1.5).

- Legacy per-frame `subtask_index` annotations are superseded by the new language columns.
- `--dataset.vcodec` was renamed to `--dataset.rgb_encoder.vcodec`, such that RGB and depth cameras video codecs may be set separately.

We present an open-source ROS 2 stack for following directional arrows, reaching a terminal cone and returning autonomously to the start. It connects YOLOv8n detection and geometric direction, range and bearing estimation with RGB-D SLAM, wheel-inertial state estimation, kinematics-aware planning, behavior-tree mission management and STM32 actuation. Standard interfaces separate reusable autonomy from the hardware layer; a proportional path-following plugin supports low-speed rover motion. Public resources include software, configuration, a labeled dataset, trained weights and evaluation logs. On 478 held-out images, the detector achieves mAP@0.5 of 0.720 under the Ultralytics evaluator and outperforms a classical OpenCV baseline under a shared evaluation protocol. The reported perception latency is 25 ms on a Jetson Orin NX. {"arxiv_id":"2606.20135","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2606.20135"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["diffusion_policy"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2606.20135v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: Flow matching has emerged as a standard paradigm for robotic manipulation owing to its strong expressive power for modelling complex, multimodal action distributions, alongside similar approaches like diffusion policy. However, existing methods rely on discretized action chunks, making them brittle to demonstrations collected at heterogeneous control frequencies and prone to temporally inconsistent actions that degrade control stability. In this paper, we propose Frequency-Aware Flow Matching (FAFM), which outputs continuous, temporally consistent actions. To handle heterogeneous frequency input, we transform discrete action sequences into the frequency domain with the discrete cosine transform (DCT), perform flow matching over the resulting coefficients, and reconstruct continuous actions via cosine basis expansion. To generate temporally consistent actions, we regularize the first-order temporal derivative to promote smooth actions. This corresponds to a Sobolev-type constraint that suppresses high-frequency errors and discourages abrupt action changes. Our FAFM is simple, introduces no additional network parameters and applies to standalone flow-matching policies and vision-language action models. Across synthetic toy benchmark, obstacle avoidance, LapGym, and LIBERO, FAFM improves success rates, multimodal expressivity, motion smoothness, convergence speed, robustness to mechanical bias and mixed-frequency input. These gains are consistent when deployed on a real-world Franka robot. Code available at https://github.com/gakakulicc/FAFM.","title":"Frequency-Aware Flow Matching for Continuous and Consistent Robotic Action Generation","title_en":"Frequency-Aware Flow Matching for Continuous and Consistent Robotic Action Generation","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20135","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

Although simulators can generate large amounts of additional data, standard simulation mixing approaches, which directly combine simulated and real experience, can degrade performance due to simulator inaccuracies, especially when they bias the solution away from the optimal policy. We propose a conservative simulation-aided learning method based on control variates, where simulated data is used solely to reduce variance in the learning process rather than directly shaping the learning target. {"arxiv_id":"2611.11940","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.11940"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.11940v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Underwater leader-follower formation control requires continuous relative-pose estimation despite degraded sensing conditions and limited onboard computation. {"arxiv_id":"2611.08372","authors":["Sateesh Kumar","Arnav Balaji","Arpit Bahety","Skand Peri","Georgios Pavlakos","Roberto Martín-Martín"],"categories":["cs.RO","cs.AI","cs.CV"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08372"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["imitation_learning"],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-05T17:50:35Z","rule_score":90,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. {"arxiv_id":"2611.13227","authors":["Renhao Zhang","Mingzhe Li","Bruno Castro da Silva"],"categories":["cs.RO","cs.CR"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.13227"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-09T20:56:25Z","rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction. Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally. LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator's behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations. We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters.","title":"Latent Barrier Steering: Hierarchical Safety for Generative Planning","title_en":"Latent Barrier Steering: Hierarchical Safety for Generative Planning","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13227v1","version":"v1","version_updated_at":"2026-11-09T20:56:25Z"}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.11516","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.11516"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":50,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.11516v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: World models allow autonomous vehicles to imagine the consequences of candidate actions before execution, but their reliability depends on the futures represented in their training data. We identify a survivorship bias in driving world models: because the futures recorded in prevailing driving datasets almost always end safely, existing models often imagine benign outcomes even when a collision is imminent. We introduce a neutral world model (NWM) that learns both routine and safety-critical futures from a mixture of routine driving and real accident videos with a bounding-box-guided objective. The NWM more faithfully anticipates imminent collisions, while maintaining a low false collision rate and competitive generation quality in routine driving. We further use the model as an imagination engine for decision-making. Given multiple ego trajectories, the NWM predicts the future associated with each candidate, and a reward function evaluates these imagined outcomes before selecting an action. On challenging NAVSIM scenarios, this procedure selects the better trajectory more reliably than the baseline world model. Zero-shot experiments with real-world pedestrian dummy crossing data collected using an autonomous research vehicle further demonstrate transfer to unseen sensor observations. These results show that correcting survivorship bias enables world models to more faithfully reason about futures and support safety-critical decision-making in autonomous driving.","title":"Breaking survivorship bias in driving world models","title_en":"Breaking survivorship bias in driving world models","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11516","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.12017","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.12017"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["diffusion_policy"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.12017v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Dexterous grasping in robotics relies on distinct hand configurations depending on object geometry. We introduce BetaGrasp, a 3D diffusion policy that conditions a DP3-style point-cloud policy on a four-class grasp label (crimp, sloper, pinch, and jug), running on a Franka arm with a 16-DoF LEAP hand. We also introduce a climbing-hold benchmark: a spring testbed whose ratchet gives a slip-force reading in newtons. In our analysis the policy's point-cloud encoder did not separate the four holds, so the scan alone gave it little to choose a grasp from. Without the label (a DP3-style baseline), simulated rollouts from the robot's reset pose all end in a jug grasp, whatever the hold (25% correct grasp type, versus 94% for BetaGrasp). {"arxiv_id":"2611.12113","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.12113"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["vla"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.12113v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: A robot that works among people must judge what it cannot see: whether an object is still where it was last seen, and whether a pull on a door or drawer is worth its risk. Maps that track object change hold nothing about force, maps of physical properties answer a risk question at a fixed risk level, and vision-language-action models keep no explicit estimate of hidden physics. We propose Motion Belief Action (MBA), a decision layer on the scene map. From how often people move an object and how much force it needs, how much load it holds and whether it is blocked, MBA chooses under a force limit to look again, nudge, open, brace or decline, with its risk set by the task's costs. On real activity in 9 kitchens, it predicts whether an object is still in place better than FreMEn and Perpetua, and decides when to look again at lower cost than these and the persistence filter, because about a quarter of placements end in a pick-up within 30 s. On real pulls of doors and drawers in 17 locations, made by a person with a force-sensing gripper, the map's force estimates decide better than a part-type average. Setting the risk from the costs also beats a published risk rule at its fixed level. In simulation, with the force limit at the training parts' median force, MBA raises SmolVLA's and Octo's scores by declining pulls; most declined door pulls would fail, but on drawers more would have opened, and a part-type average gets about half of this gain. In both, a published risk rule set to the risk these costs imply is MBA's rule for a single pull and decides as well in the main settings. A link between opening and holding force, a probing nudge and an action prior for camera tracking do not help in the main settings, and over the real-pull sweep the nudge costs a little.","title":"Motion Belief Action: From a Visual Scene Map to Physical Decisions","title_en":"Motion Belief Action: From a Visual Scene Map to Physical Decisions","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12113","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2607.06724","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2607.06724"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":50,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2607.06724v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: LLM-based robot planners are fluent but cannot guarantee that their plans are executable or safe. Classical PDDL planners can guarantee symbolic validity, but only once the problem is fully specified, and they make poor use of an LLM's ability to read context and repair plans. We present EvoPlan, a neuro-symbolic framework whose guarantees are symbolic validity and satisfaction of a constraint learned from data. The planner works with locally-hosted open-weight models, so it does not require a cloud service. EvoPlan has three parts. First, an offline procedure that mines a single global Signal Temporal Logic (STL) mobility constraint from demonstrations. Perturbed demonstrations supply the missing negatives without encoding any rule, and evolutionary search fits the constraint, which captures driving rules or social-navigation preferences within a modelled taxonomy of norms. We use the mined constraint to shield driving and navigation policies on Bench2Drive and HA-VLN-CE. Second, an evolutionary PDDL planner: an LLM proposes and repairs plans, programmatic validators decide which ones survive, and the validated portion of the plan grows over iterations. On open-world ALFWorld and NL-PDDL Blocksworld, it approaches classical planning when the goal vocabulary agrees with the action model, and it stays robust when the two disagree and classical planning fails. Third, a constrained execution loop: Nav2 uses the costmap to ground the plan into waypoints, which are checked against the mined constraint. Violations and execution failures update the PDDL problem for re-planning. We demonstrate the full pipeline in Gazebo and on a Clearpath Jackal robot. More details and videos are on the project page: https://nbhavyasai.github.io/evoplan/","title":"EvoPlan: Evolutionary Neuro-Symbolic Robot Planning with Spatio-Temporal Guarantees","title_en":"EvoPlan: Evolutionary Neuro-Symbolic Robot Planning with Spatio-Temporal Guarantees","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06724","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.10635","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.10635"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["imitation_learning"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.10635v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Reliable navigation with a single monocular limited field-of-view camera is challenging because the lack of depth measurements and limited spatial awareness complicate collision checking. Existing approaches to tackle these challenges fall into two categories. Model-based planners can incorporate explicit collision-avoidance guidance which leads to better generalization but are often computationally expensive and require manual tuning of the algorithmic parameters. In contrast, end-to-end approaches trained by imitation learning can be flexible but typically encode safety only implicitly and thus can suffer from high collision rates in novel scenarios.\n  In this paper, we present a middle ground through model-based imitation learning. The model-based part is a learned collision model that can map a sequence of past images and a candidate control sequence to a distribution of worst-case obstacle clearance. This predictive distribution in turn is used to define a collision-risk cost in a trajectory optimization formulation. The imitation component uses human demonstrations to learn scene-dependent balancing of collision risk with other task costs such as goal progress. We also use it to learn the algorithmic parameters (e.g., a warm start) of our optimizer to accelerate the solution process. We show that our approach can demonstrate highly reliable navigation in cluttered environments on robots with different embodiments. We also demonstrate a substantial reduction in collision rate over recent end-to-end and model-based baselines.","title":"Model-Based Imitation Learning For Monocular Vision-Based Navigation","title_en":"Model-Based Imitation Learning For Monocular Vision-Based Navigation","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10635","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2605.30326","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2605.30326"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2605.30326v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: The ability to reason, adapt, and creatively solve problems under unexpected challenges is essential for robots operating in real-world environments. However, current robotic benchmarks primarily emphasize skill-level execution and provide limited insight into such cognitive reasoning capabilities. We introduce RoboWits, a bi-manual robotic benchmark designed to systematically evaluate cognitive reasoning, creative tool use, and robustness to unexpected conditions. To enable scalable construction of high-quality reasoning-centric unexpected scenarios, we propose an automated task generation pipeline formulated as a multi-agent cooperative framework, comprising agents for seed task generation and verification, metric generation, scene generation, and task mutation. Using the pipeline, we curated 30 diverse seed tasks and 200 tasks with mutations and graded difficulty across geometry, material, and assembly-based reasoning. We benchmark popular robot policies, pre-trained VLAs, a zero-shot policy built on a frontier VLM, and oracle-state planners.\n  Our results reveal a significant performance gap: while pre-trained VLAs exhibit preliminary success on seed tasks after fine-tuning, they struggle to perform on mutated tasks, implying their brittleness in manipulation tasks requiring reasoning, strategy adaptation, and robustness to deceptive or constrained environments. {"arxiv_id":"2605.10707","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2605.10707"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":50,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2605.10707v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: Object-centric view planning is a core component of active geometric 3D reconstruction in robotics, yet existing evaluations often conflate object complexity, planning difficulty, budget assumptions, and physical reachability constraints. As a result, conclusions drawn from idealized view-planning evaluations may not reliably predict performance under realistic reconstruction settings. We introduce ObjView-Bench, an evaluation framework for rethinking difficulty and deployment in object-centric view planning. First, we disentangle three quantities underlying view-planning evaluation: omnidirectional self-occlusion as an object-side attribute, observation saturation difficulty, and protocol-dependent planning difficulty defined through a set-cover formulation. This separation supports controlled dataset construction, analysis of slow-saturation objects, and a case study showing that planning difficulty-aware sampling can improve learned view planners. Second, we design deployment-oriented evaluation protocols that reveal how budget regimes and reachable-view constraints alter method behavior. Across classical, learned, and hybrid planners, ObjView-Bench shows that difficulty, budget, and reachability constraints substantially change method rankings and failure modes. Project page: https://objview-bench.github.io/","title":"ObjView-Bench: Rethinking Difficulty and Deployment for Object-Centric View Planning","title_en":"ObjView-Bench: Rethinking Difficulty and Deployment for Object-Centric View Planning","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10707","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.08209","authors":["Satvik Sharma","Hengyuan Hu","Mihika Kamat","Dorsa Sadigh","Jeannette Bohg"],"categories":["cs.RO"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08209"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-05T16:00:16Z","rule_score":90,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). We introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks across three embodiments designed to test in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning for precise control. The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%. Specifically, leveraging statistical theory, we develop an asymptotically unbiased and $\\sqrt {n}$-consistent PnP estimator that accounts for varying 3D triangulation uncertainties, ensuring that the relative pose estimate converges to the ground truth as the number of features increases. {"arxiv_id":"2611.08361","authors":["Aditya Iyer","Andy Ye","Akshay Narayan","Nora Ayanian"],"categories":["cs.RO","cs.MA"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08361"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-05T17:41:02Z","rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"Cooperative localization uses odometry and inter-robot measurements to estimate the motion of a robot team. These measurements describe only relative geometry, but the team's estimated position and orientation can drift together over time, i.e., gauge drift. In this work, we study correction of this gauge drift using a radio attenuation map registered in the same world coordinate frame used for robot poses. Specifically, we propose Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI), an interface that converts power residuals and their pose derivatives into a Gaussian information matrix and vector pair. RPI builds on the insight that received power is sensitive to shared displacement in the world map. The pose estimator uses the interface together with odometry and inter-robot measurements to update poses and minimize uncertainty. We characterize the shared motions detectable from the map and observed links. For an uncertain shared map, RPI keeps correlations across robots and time and reproduces joint Gaussian pose estimates and covariances. Across $1000$ simulated Gaussian trials, RPI matches the results of joint estimation. Across 32 paired trials with a registered map, RPI reduces common-position RMSE from $0.542$m to $0.140$m in a $50\\times50$m arena compared with a baseline that uses radio only to weight relative measurements.","title":"Radio-to-Pose Information for Gauge-Drift Correction in Cooperative Localization","title_en":"Radio-to-Pose Information for Gauge-Drift Correction in Cooperative Localization","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08361v1","version":"v1","version_updated_at":"2026-11-05T17:41:02Z"}

{"arxiv_id":"2604.07677","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2604.07677"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2604.07677v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: Spatial single-loop mechanisms such as Bennett linkages offer a unique combination of one-degree-of-freedom actuation and nontrivial spatial trajectories, making them attractive for lightweight bio-inspired robotic design. However, existing synthesis methods rely on dual quaternion algebra and rational motion interpolation and factorization, placing task-based linkage design outside the reach of most engineers, a gap addressed by the Rational Linkages library recently developed by the authors. This paper presents a bird-inspired flapping-wing mechanism built from two coupled spatial four-bars, driven by a single motor. One linkage is actuated to generate the desired spatial sweeping stroke, while the serially coupled linkage remains unactuated and passively switches between extended and folded wing configurations over the stroke cycle. Additionally, we introduce a simplified kinematic methodology for constructing Bennett linkages from quadrilaterals that contain a desired surface area and further leverage mechanically induced passive state switching. By jointly modeling action generation and future observation prediction, WAMs can act and anticipate the outcomes of the actions. However, existing WAMs typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders trained with reconstruction, which may not produce representations well suited for robot control. In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning physicallygrounded, control-relevant representations for WAMs. We propose MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns latent representations of multisensory observations end-to-end with a diffusion backbone. While naive joint training can lead to feature collapse, MDF++ introduces a multi-task learning strategy that leverages cross-modal correlations to learn task-relevant representations. {"arxiv_id":"2611.00405","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.00405"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":50,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.00405v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: Data flywheels promise continuous improvement via insights from deployment data. Understanding how the deployed model succeeds and fails can steer subsequent data collection towards patching failures and reinforcing successes. However, robot deployments create large volumes of high-dimensional rollout data, which is challenging to understand and confidently ground data collection decisions in. To make deployment data easier to analyze and act on, we propose behavior graphs, which compress policy rollouts into a single interpretable, directed graph. We construct the graphs by learning to identify similar behavior modes across rollouts, connecting the behaviors temporally, and finally linking them to outcomes. In a user study on three real-world tasks, where participants analyzed rollouts to choose a data collection strategy, 16 of 18 preferred behavior graphs to rollout videos, reaching comparable conclusions with 40.3% lower perceived temporal demand and 37.6% lower effort. Beyond interpretability for deployment data, behavior graphs are capable progress predictors: across 43 datasets, they improve the rank correlation between predicted progress and true temporal order by 22.9% and reduce mean absolute error by 53.5% relative to the strongest baseline. As the number of deployed robots grows, behavior graphs lend structure to high-dimensional policy rollouts and make deployment data easier to interpret and reason about.","title":"Behavior Graphs: Unsupervised Graph Structures for Interpreting Robot Deployment Data","title_en":"Behavior Graphs: Unsupervised Graph Structures for Interpreting Robot Deployment Data","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00405","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

A freely held pen instead couples grasp stability, tip motion, and contact force. We present Grip, Trace, Write, a force-aware simulation environment and learning framework for high-DoF handwriting. A two-branch actor separates pen retention from arm-wrist writing while preserving their closed-loop coupling. Training learns a grasp controller, initializes writing from inverse-kinematics demonstrations by behavior cloning, and improves writing through reinforcement learning with rewards on ink, force, time, and retention. {"arxiv_id":"2606.23431","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2606.23431"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2606.23431v2 Announce Type: replace \nAbstract: Fine-grained, bimanual dexterous manipulation remains a foundational challenge in robotics. Embodiment gaps hinder accurate kinematic mapping, and visual tracking alone does not regulate contact forces. To address these limitations, we propose a tactile-driven adaptation strategy designed to enable fine-grained manipulation on top of teleoperation pipelines. Instantiated within our bimanual dexterous framework, DexTeleop-0, this strategy introduces a real-time optimization loop that adds robot-side contact corrections to human tracking commands using fingertip feedback. By estimating contact positions and forces, the system dynamically computes localized corrections using a contact-stiffness approximation and the kinematic Jacobian, with per-contact vector force tracking, soft predicted-contact-moment regularization, and bounded hand-joint residuals. We evaluate this tactile-driven adaptation strategy across both simulated environments and real-world hardware. Controlled simulation replay yields final-stage success rates of 91% for Ball Assembly and 62% for Stir in Cup, versus 88% and 49% for force tracking alone. {"arxiv_id":"2604.08410","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2604.08410"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2604.08410v3 Announce Type: replace-cross \nAbstract: In industrial assembly, equipment maintenance, and everyday tool-use scenarios, robots need not only to grasp objects stably but also to establish task-appropriate contact configurations according to task intentions and tool functionality. However, existing methods lack explicit mappings from open-vocabulary instructions to 3D functional contact structures and dexterous grasp configurations, limiting robots' adaptability to diverse tools and functional tasks. To address this limitation, we propose BLaFA (Bridging Language to 3D Functional Affordances for Dexterous Robotic Grasping), a structured framework for language-driven functional dexterous grasping. First, a Knowledge-guided Language Parsing (KLP) module leverages structured knowledge to transform natural-language instructions into semantic sextuples of manipulation constraints. Second, a 3D Gaussian Splatting based hierarchical semantic representation and a Triangular Functional Point Localization (TriLocation) module are developed to localize 3D functional contact keypoints under task-tool topology constraints. Finally, a 3D Keypoint Grasp Matrix Transformation (KGT3D+) module maps the localized keypoints and semantic constraints to executable wrist poses and finger-level joint and force commands. Evaluations on 100 open-vocabulary language instructions, 14 task-tool combinations covering four functional intents, and real-world robotic experiments in representative scenes demonstrate that BLaFA can effectively translate natural-language instructions into task-aligned 3D functional contact structures and corresponding dexterous grasps, thereby enabling language-driven robotic tool use across diverse tasks. The source code will be made publicly available. Code will be publicly available at https://github.com/PopeyePxx/BLaFA.","title":"BLaFA: Bridging Language to 3D Functional Affordances for Dexterous Robotic Grasping in Tool Use","title_en":"BLaFA: Bridging Language to 3D Functional Affordances for Dexterous Robotic Grasping in Tool Use","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08410","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.","title":"HaNDF: Object-Conditioned Geometric Neural Hand Distance Fields","title_en":"HaNDF: Object-Conditioned Geometric Neural Hand Distance Fields","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08578","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

{"arxiv_id":"2611.12678","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.12678"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":50,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.12678v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.","title":"Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model","title_en":"Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12678","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

To reduce coordination demands, a time-varying predicted conflict graph selects relevant pairwise interactions. The associated collision-avoidance constraints are convexified once per MPC update using warm-start trajectories, yielding a fixed convex quadratic program (QP). The resulting QP is then decomposed using an edge-consensus formulation of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), enabling parallel robot-local optimization and independent closed-form projections onto separating half-spaces. {"arxiv_id":"2611.13271","authors":["Yuan Fang","Long Zhuang","Lingzi Xing","Xijia Wei","Jingqi Jiang","Fangzhan Shi","Simon Julier","Kevin Chetty"],"categories":["cs.RO","cs.CV"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.13271"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2026-11-09T21:36:59Z","rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides weather-robust sensing and direct Doppler measurements, yet automotive perception pipelines often reduce its output to sparse point clouds or two-dimensional projections, leaving raw range-azimuth-Doppler (RAD) cubes underutilized. Ego motion induces Doppler responses from world-static structures, while Doppler wrapping aliases radial velocities, complicating moving-object detection and velocity estimation. We present RaMOD (Radar-based Moving-Object Detection), a real-time framework for moving-object detection and velocity estimation from raw RAD cubes acquired by a vehicle-mounted single-chip radar. RaMOD explicitly estimates frame-wise ego motion and uses the estimated radar translational velocity to predict the Doppler region of world-static structures and suppress returns within it. It temporally encodes the suppressed cubes into multi-scale features to predict RAD-space boxes with class labels. For each detected object, it predicts radial and forward velocities under raw-Doppler and Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping probabilities. On our BRIDGE-Liv dataset, RaMOD outperforms all compared raw-radar methods across RAD-cube, RA, and RD detection settings, achieving 80.8% cube mAP at IoU 0.30, 15.7 percentage points above the strongest RAD-cube baseline. {"arxiv_id":"2405.12213","authors":["Octo Model Team","Dibya Ghosh","Homer Walke","Karl Pertsch","Kevin Black","Oier Mees","Sudeep Dasari","Joey Hejna","Tobias Kreiman","Charles Xu","Jianlan Luo","You Liang Tan","Lawrence Yunliang Chen","Pannag Sanketi","Quan Vuong","Ted Xiao","Dorsa Sadigh","Chelsea Finn","Sergey Levine"],"categories":["cs.RO","cs.LG"],"claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2405.12213"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":[],"publication_date_basis":"arxiv_first_submission","published_at":"2024-05-20T17:57:01Z","rule_score":70,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"Large policies pretrained on diverse robot datasets have the potential to transform robotic learning: instead of training new policies from scratch, such generalist robot policies may be finetuned with only a little in-domain data, yet generalize broadly. However, to be widely applicable across a range of robotic learning scenarios, environments, and tasks, such policies need to handle diverse sensors and action spaces, accommodate a variety of commonly used robotic platforms, and finetune readily and efficiently to new domains. In this work, we aim to lay the groundwork for developing open-source, widely applicable, generalist policies for robotic manipulation. As a first step, we introduce Octo, a large transformer-based policy trained on 800k trajectories from the Open X-Embodiment dataset, the largest robot manipulation dataset to date. It can be instructed via language commands or goal images and can be effectively finetuned to robot setups with new sensory inputs and action spaces within a few hours on standard consumer GPUs. In experiments across 9 robotic platforms, we demonstrate that Octo serves as a versatile policy initialization that can be effectively finetuned to new observation and action spaces. {"arxiv_id":"2611.11127","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.11127"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["reinforcement_learning"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":80,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.11127v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: We present a pipeline for transferring Awa Odori, a traditional Japanese festival dance, from monocular video to a commercial Unitree G1 EDU humanoid. The pipeline combines human mesh recovery, kinematic retargeting, reinforcement learning for motion tracking in simulation, and onboard deployment via ONNX. Training ran on a single RTX 5070 GPU. An eleven-version deployment ladder evaluated on hardware examines three interventions. We detect and repair silent corruption of deployment artifacts, model state-estimator drift during training, and edit the reference motion to support stable execution and a controlled ending. It is specifically designed to achieve high throughput in scenes involving collisions among large numbers of detailed meshes. Its predecessor, Lodos-v1, had two main limitations. First, it solved the standard convex relaxation of cone-complementarity-based contact dynamics, thereby inheriting well-known physical artifacts, including lift-off and artificial compliance in the normal direction, as well as creep in the tangential direction. Second, its contact-group reparameterization scheme, which rescales spring-damper forces using a single factor per collision pair, could not be integrated with other constraints required by a full-fledged simulator, such as joint limits and welds. These decisions are difficult because their correctness often depends on how a scene evolves, such as whether an approaching car is slowing or a cyclist will cross the robot's path. Vision-language models (VLMs) can interpret such cues, but they reason over images that lack metric geometry and motion. Supplying this evidence at every step is too slow for real-time navigation, and hand-crafted triggers cannot anticipate the open-ended variety of outdoor situations. We present MOSU2, a long-range navigation system with two-stage trajectory selection, in which first-stage contextual reasoning determines when additional evidence is needed and what to retrieve. Only when an interaction remains unresolved does the first stage trigger the second stage to retrieve geometric and dynamic information and align it with scene context to make navigation decisions. Building on MOSU, MOSU2 follows routes from GPS-based route planning and filters candidate trajectories through multi-modal traversability analysis before selecting a trajectory to move the robot. In real-world experiments spanning stop gestures, construction sites, crosswalks, and roads shared with vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians, MOSU2 raises mean navigation success from 61.8% to 94.2% and condition-detection accuracy from 72.2% to 91.4% over its single-image predecessor, at about 2.2 times its mean decision latency. {"arxiv_id":"2611.08895","claims_status":"author_claims_not_independently_reproduced","date_note":"RSS announcement is not the original submission date; API verification is pending.","doi":null,"evidence_scope":"abstract_and_metadata_only","feed_announced_at":"Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500","identifiers":{"arxiv":"2611.08895"},"kind":"preprint","method_tags":["vla"],"publication_date_basis":"unknown","published_at":null,"rule_score":60,"selection_reason":"规则排序（非 AI、非质量评审）：官方来源 +20；有摘要/发行说明 +20；明确版本 +10；每个匹配子领域 +10（最多 +40）。","summary":"arXiv:2611.08895v1 Announce Type: new \nAbstract: Operators can state safety constraints for robots as prohibitions such as \"do not put the bowl on the stove\". We study whether OpenVLA follows such prohibitions and where it represents the goal it executes. The 10 tasks of LIBEROGoal share one scene, so we can label the goal that each rollout executes. We combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors. On LIBERO-Goal, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed. The model executed the forbidden task in 79% of negated rollouts and completed 78% of plain tasks. A goal probe gives similar read-outs under \"not X\" and \"X\". Activation patching shows that the first action depends mostly on the instruction tokens before layer 12 and on the last prompt token from layer 16 onward. A fixed steering vector at the instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12 of 18 rollouts. Fixed vectors and prefill patches at layers 12 to 20 redirected none of 158. From layer 16, only patches at every decoded action token redirected the robot (15 of 18 rollouts at layer 24). When the instruction changes during a rollout, the layer-32 goal read-out detects non-compliance better than failure detectors, and an external probe on image and instruction features performs comparably. These results support enforcing prohibitions outside the instruction and monitoring goal read-outs against the specification. Goal edits in OpenVLA should act before layer 12 or patch every action token.","title":"Localizing and Editing the Goal Representation of a Vision-Language-Action Model","title_en":"Localizing and Editing the Goal Representation of a Vision-Language-Action Model","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08895","version":null,"version_updated_at":null}

However, existing six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) pose recovery approaches often require pre-calibrated workspace field maps or iterative nonlinear optimization. This letter presents a Gradiometer-Based Electromagnetic Localization System (GELS), a closed-form tracking framework that uses a compact magnetometer array as an embedded quasi-gradiometer to estimate local magnetic fields and gradient tensors. These quantities are mapped by the Euler homogeneous relation to displacements between source and array, from which Procrustes registration over multiple sources recovers the array orientation and position using at least three noncollinear sources. The algorithm requires known source positions and array geometry, but no pre-calibrated workspace field maps, initial pose guesses, or calibrated source magnetic moments. The recovered \\added[]{array} pose also enables a demonstration of sublevel dipole localization by serving as a mobile magnetic reference frame. Benchtop experiments across sensor array configurations and excitation modes validate the proposed closed-form 6-DoF localization pipeline, with a median solver runtime of \\SI{172.00}{\\micro\\second}.
